questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Slope of the Tangent Line to a Curve Given in Implicit Form at a Point
questions.problem: Find the slope of the tangent at the point $(2,\frac{\pi }{4})$ for the curve $x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)=\sqrt{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the slope at a point, we use implicit differentiation to calculate the derivative of the curve, assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the $x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{2}) \\ x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(y))+\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x) & =0 \\ x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(y) & =0 \\ x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(y) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)}{x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡(y)}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

The slope of the tangent at the point $(2,\frac{\pi }{4})$ is then given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}_{(2,\pi /4)} \\  & ={(-\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡(y)}{x})}_{(2,\pi /4)} \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})}{2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Derivative of a Function Given in Implicit Form Using the Product Rule
questions.worked_solution:
First, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the $x\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)+{y}^{3}=2{x}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)+{y}^{3}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y))+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}^{3}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3}) \\ [x(\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)]+3{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6{x}^{2} \\ x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)+3{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now we solve the equation for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+3{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6{x}^{2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(y) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)+3{y}^{2}) & =6{x}^{2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(y) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{6{x}^{2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)}{x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)+3{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Derivative of a Function Given in Implicit Form Using the Product Rule
questions.worked_solution:
First, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the ${x}^{3}{e}^{y}$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}{e}^{y} & =9{x}^{4} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3}{e}^{y}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(9{x}^{4}) \\ [({x}^{3})({e}^{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})+(3{x}^{2})({e}^{y})] & =36{x}^{3} \\ {x}^{3}\,{e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+3{x}^{2}{e}^{y} & =36{x}^{3}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now we solve the equation for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}{e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+3{x}^{2}{e}^{y} & =36{x}^{3} \\ {x}^{3}{e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =36{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}{e}^{y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{36{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}{e}^{y}}{{x}^{3}{e}^{y}} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{36}{{e}^{y}}-\frac{3}{x}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Slope of the Tangent Line to a Curve Given in Implicit Form at a Point
questions.worked_solution:
To find the slope at a point, we use implicit differentiation to calculate the derivative of the curve, assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the ${x}^{2}{y}^{2}$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}2{y}^{3}+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-{x}^{3} & =2 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{y}^{3}+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-{x}^{3}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{y}^{3})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}{y}^{2})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2) \\ 6{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+[2x{y}^{2}+2{x}^{2}y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}]-3{x}^{2} & =0 \\ 6{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2x{y}^{2}+2{x}^{2}y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3{x}^{2} & =0 \\ (6{y}^{2}+2{x}^{2}y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2}-2x{y}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{3{x}^{2}-2x{y}^{2}}{6{y}^{2}+2{x}^{2}y}\end{aligned}
$$

The slope of the tangent at the point $(1,1)$ is then given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{(1,1)} \\  & ={(\frac{3{x}^{2}-2x{y}^{2}}{6{y}^{2}+2{x}^{2}y})|}_{(1,1)} \\  & =\frac{3(1)^{2}-2(1)(1)^{2}}{6(1)^{2}+2(1)^{2}(1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining an Intercept of a Tangent or Normal Line to a Curve Given in Implicit Form
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13951578/assets/d997ec4e099fc8be5b34a51bdfd0e9511915c348671d9832ed640f0ec4360602.png)

The equation $4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=15y$ represents an ellipse. The normal line at the point $(3,3)$ on the ellipse intersects the $x$-axis at the point $P.$ What are the coordinates of $P?$

The coordinates of $P$ are $($
{{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}}$).$
questions.worked_solution:
First of all, we need to find the slope of the normal line at the point $(3,3).$ Remember that the slope of the normal line, ${m}^{′},$ is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line:

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we will calculate the derivative using implicit differentiation, assuming that $y=y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =15y \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(15y) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(15y) \\ 8x+2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =15\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \\ 2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-15\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-8x \\ (2y-15)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-8x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{8x}{2y-15}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at the point $(3,3)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{(3,\,3)} \\  & ={(-\frac{8x}{2y-15})|}_{(3,\,3)} \\  & =-\frac{8\cdot 3}{2\cdot 3-15} \\  & =-\frac{24}{(-9)} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{(\frac{8}{3})}=-\frac{3}{8}.
$$

We can write the equation of the normal line at the point $(3,3)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & ={m}^{′}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-3 & =-\frac{3}{8}(x-3) \\ y & =-\frac{3}{8}x+\frac{9}{8}+3 \\ y & =-\frac{3}{8}x+\frac{33}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we just need to find where this normal line intersects the $x$-axis. At the point $P$ the $y$-coordinate is $0,$ so we set $y=0$ and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{3}{8}x+\frac{33}{8} \\ 0 & =-\frac{3}{8}x+\frac{33}{8} \\ \frac{3}{8}x & =\frac{33}{8} \\ x & =11\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(11,\,0).$
